title: What 1,866 popular GitHub projects tell their AI coding agents
content:
You join a project and open its AGENTS.md before your first task, the way your coding agent will. It starts well: what the project is, how to run the tests. Then it keeps going. Code style. Commit format. A section of lessons learned, each one a mistake someone corrected once. “Always validate input.” “Never edit generated files.” “Keep changes small.” Two hundred lines in, you notice you are skimming.
Your agent does not skim. It reads every line at the start of every session, and then it does what most of us do with a long list of rules: it follows most of them, most of the time.
Researchers have started to study these files. One study catalogued what 2,303 of them contain (opens in a new tab). Another, at ETH Zurich, found (opens in a new tab) that developer-written files raise an agent’s success rate only marginally while adding up to 19% to its cost, and advised that they “describe only minimal requirements”. We asked a different question: of the rules in these files, how many are enforced? To find out, we wrote a script to collect and analyse every agent instruction file in 1,866 of the most popular active projects on GitHub.
One in three popular GitHub projects now ships an instruction file for AI coding agents, and AGENTS.md is the common format. Half of the main files run past 100 lines. In a random sample classified rule by rule, three in five rules could be checked by a script, at least in part, yet fewer than one rule in twenty names the check. Most rules rely on the agent remembering.
The short version
- 627 of 1,866 projects (34%) ship at least one agent instruction file. In TypeScript projects it is 73%; in Perl, 4%.
- AGENTS.md is the common ground. 78% of those projects have one, against 52% with CLAUDE.md and 20% with GitHub Copilot’s instructions.
- Half the main files are longer than 100 lines (302 of 582). The median is 106 lines, about 850 words.
- Three in five rules could be checked by a script, at least in part (157 of 257 in a classified sample).
- Fewer than one rule in twenty names its check (16 of 431 across two classified samples, 3.7%).
- About 30 projects keep two separate rulebooks, an AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md with different content.
- Stale maps are rare. About 2% of files point at a path or script that no longer exists.
How we did it
We took the projects in the public GitHub Ranking (opens in a new tab) lists of the most-starred repositories, overall and for 24 languages, on 15 October 2026: 2,424 projects, of which 1,867 had commits this year and 1,866 could be read. For each one we listed every file at the latest commit and read its agent instruction files: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, GitHub Copilot’s instructions, and Cursor and Windsurf rules.
A script measured what can be counted exactly: which files exist, how long they are, what their headings cover. Anything that needs judgement, such as whether a line is really a rule or whether a script could check it, was classified one rule at a time on random samples by a separate AI reviewer, independent of the script, and those are the figures we report. The method and its limits are at the end.
One project in three now writes for its agents
627 of the 1,866 projects (34%) have at least one agent instruction file.
AGENTS.md has become the shared format: 489 of the 627 projects (78%) have one, and 214 have nothing else. CLAUDE.md appears in 328, GitHub Copilot’s instructions in 123, Cursor rules in 28 and GEMINI.md in 27. Most projects with a CLAUDE.md also have an AGENTS.md, which matters later.
Adoption depends heavily on the language.
TypeScript leads at 73%, then Go (58%), Rust (52%) and Python (49%). At the other end are Elixir (19%), Haskell (15%) and Perl (4%). Our guess is that this follows where coding agents are used most, but the data cannot show why.
What the files cover
We grouped the headings of each main file by topic.
Three in five files give the commands to build and run, describe the structure of the code and set out its style; about half cover testing. Only about one in eight has a section on security, and one in sixteen on performance. The Agent READMEs study (opens in a new tab) also found both rarely covered, in a different sample: security in 14.8% of files and performance in 14.5%.
How long they are
The median main file is 106 lines and about 850 words, roughly 1,600 tokens by the usual rule of thumb of four characters to a token. The longest tenth run past 3,000 words. 302 of 582 files (52%) are longer than 100 lines, 87 are longer than 300, and the longest is 1,048 lines.
Length has a cost. In a study of 124 pull requests (opens in a new tab), an AGENTS.md cut the median time Codex took by about 29%, but the ETH Zurich study found that context files also make agents take more steps and spend more. Why 100 lines? OpenAI’s Codex team describes (opens in a new tab) giving the agent “a map, not a 1,000-page instruction manual”: an AGENTS.md of roughly 100 lines that points into the docs. Every line in the file competes with the line the agent needs for the task in front of it.
What the rules say
We took a random sample of 300 lines that read as rules and had a separate AI reviewer classify each one. 257 were real rules; the rest were fragments such as “migrations must:” or “Never”, or plain description.
No single topic dominates. Code style is the largest group (16%), followed closely by rules about how the agent should work and communicate (15%) and project-specific correctness, such as which API to call or how a value must be handled (13%). Rules about security, dependencies and generated files are each under 3% of the sample.
How many rules name their check
For each of those 257 rules we asked two questions: could a script, linter, test or CI job catch a violation, and does the rule say which one?
64 rules (25%) could be checked completely, and another 93 (36%) partly, so three in five could have a check behind them. Only 8 of those 157 name it. An earlier sample of 200 lines, classified in a separate review pass, gave the same picture: 8 of 174 rules named a check. Across both samples it is 16 of 431 rules, 3.7%.
The rest rely on the agent remembering. Some are easy to enforce and simply do not say how, like these three from the sample:
- “Don’t use empty destructuring patterns.” (one lint rule)
- “File names should be lower case with words separated by hyphens” (a short script)
- “Do not add Co-Authored-By: Claude or any Claude attribution to commit messages.” (a commit hook)
The best files show how cheap the fix is. Homebrew’s AGENTS.md is 72 lines. It opens with the one command to run before asking for input, lists the checks required before each commit, and several of its rules say what enforces them: “Never use T.must (enforced by Sorbet/ForbidTMust)”. Its commit-style rule explains that a GitHub Actions workflow rejects the wrong format. A rule written like that tells the agent what will happen if it forgets, and the check catches it if the agent forgets anyway.
Two rulebooks in one repository
209 projects keep both an AGENTS.md and a CLAUDE.md at the root. Most handle it well: in 157 of them one file simply points to the other, and five are identical copies. But about 30 keep two genuinely separate files, with different rules for different agents in the same codebase.
That is two maps of the same ground, and nothing keeps them in step. An agent reading one file follows rules the other agent never sees. If you need more than one file, make the second a one-line pointer to the first.
Rules in the folders, not just at the root
187 of the 627 projects (30%) keep instruction files in subfolders, a median of three per project and, in one case, 190. Rules for one part of the code live next to that code, and an agent working elsewhere never loads them. For large codebases it is probably the right shape: a short map at the root, and detail where the detail belongs.

report.summary: A scan of 1,866 top GitHub projects finds one in three ships an AGENTS.md-style file for AI coding agents, yet under 4% of their rules name an automated check.
report.background: Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Copilot read repository-level instruction files at the start of every session, and AGENTS.md has become the de facto shared format. As adoption spread, researchers began measuring whether these files actually help. One study catalogued the contents of 2,303 such files; a separate ETH Zurich study found developer-written context files raise an agent's success rate only marginally while adding up to 19% to cost, and recommended describing minimal requirements only. OpenAI's Codex team similarly advises a map of roughly 100 lines that points into real documentation rather than a long manual. This analysis pulled 1,866 readable, actively committed repositories from a public GitHub ranking across 24 languages, measured countable facts by script, and had an independent AI reviewer classify rule-level questions on random samples.
key_points: Adoption is mainstream but uneven: 627 of 1,866 projects (34%) ship at least one agent instruction file. AGENTS.md leads with 78% of those projects, ahead of CLAUDE.md (52%) and GitHub Copilot instructions (20%). TypeScript projects reach 73%, Go 58%, Rust 52% and Python 49%, while Perl sits at 4%.

Files are long. The median main file is 106 lines, roughly 850 words or about 1,600 tokens, and 52% exceed 100 lines, with the longest at 1,048 lines. Because every line competes with the task context, long files crowd out what the agent actually needs.

Rules are mostly unenforced. Of 257 sampled rules, three in five could be caught at least partly by a linter, test or CI job, but only 8 named the check; across two samples just 16 of 431 rules (3.7%) did. The rest depend on the model remembering.

Coverage skews to the mundane: code style (16%), how the agent should work and communicate (15%) and project-specific correctness (13%). Security, dependencies and generated files each fall under 3%; only about one in eight files has a security section and one in sixteen covers performance.

Duplication and organisation matter. 209 projects keep both AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, and around 30 hold genuinely different rulebooks with nothing keeping them in sync. 30% place instruction files in subfolders. Stale paths were rarer than expected, around 2%. Homebrew's 72-line file is held up as a model for naming its enforcers.
report.impact: The finding reframes how teams should treat agent instruction files: as executable policy rather than prose advice. For the AI industry it points toward tooling that lints, diffs and validates these files, and toward agents that surface which rules were actually checked. For developers, the cheap win is converting rules into lint rules, hooks and CI jobs, and keeping the file near 100 lines with a single source of truth per repository. For regular users, better-enforced rules mean fewer regressions and more predictable output from agent-written code, while unenforced style essays mostly add token cost and latency without measurable quality gains.
report.tools: Watch AGENTS.md as the shared convention, with Claude Code's CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules and Copilot instructions as per-tool variants that should point back to one file. For enforcement, pair ESLint, RuboCop, Sorbet's ForbidTMust-style checks, pre-commit, husky or lefthook commit hooks and GitHub Actions workflows. The Agent READMEs catalogue and the ETH Zurich context-file study are useful follow-up reading, and Codex's guidance on keeping AGENTS.md to roughly 100 lines is a practical template.
